written.q: Explain what happens inside one artificial neuron and relate each part to a biological neuron.
written.a: Aggregation: z = Σ wixi + b (weights scale inputs, bias shifts the total). Activation: a = f(z) decides how strongly it fires. Dendrites = inputs, synapse strength = weights, cell body = the sum, axon hillock (threshold about −55 mV) = activation function and bias, axon = output. Biological neurons obey the all-or-none law; activation functions are a smoother version.

written.q: Why must hidden layers use a non-linear activation function? Illustrate with an example.
written.a: Without it, stacked layers collapse into a single linear function: layer 1 z1 = 2x + 1, layer 2 z2 = 3z1 − 2 gives 6x + 1, one straight line, however deep the network. A non-linear activation bends the signal so the network can fit curves and complex boundaries.

written.q: Compare linear, sigmoid, tanh and ReLU: formula, range, typical use and main weakness.
written.a: Linear f(z) = z, range −∞ to +∞, output layer for regression, collapses layers if hidden. Sigmoid 1/(1+e−z), 0 to 1, output layer for binary classification, vanishing gradient and not zero-centred. Tanh, −1 to 1, zero-centred but still vanishing gradient. ReLU max(0, z), 0 to +∞, cheap and no vanishing gradient for z > 0 so the default in hidden layers; weakness: dying ReLU.

written.q: Describe how a neural network learns: forward pass, loss, backpropagation, gradient descent and epochs.
written.a: Start with small random weights. Forward pass: data flows to the output giving a prediction. Loss: measure the error (SSR). Backpropagation: using the chain rule, work backward to get the slope of the loss for every weight and bias. Gradient descent: new value = old value − learning rate × slope. Repeat; one epoch is a full pass over the training data, and many epochs are needed.

written.q: One sigmoid neuron has weights w<sub>0</sub> = w<sub>1</sub> = w<sub>2</sub> = 0, inputs x<sub>1</sub> = x<sub>2</sub> = 1 (and x<sub>0</sub> = 1), target 1, learning rate 1, E = (y − ŷ)². Perform one update.
written.a: z = 0, ŷ = 0.5, E = 0.25. Slope per weight = −2(y − ŷ)ŷ(1 − ŷ)x = −2 × 0.5 × 0.25 × 1 = −0.25. New w = 0 − 1 × (−0.25) = 0.25 each. New z = 0.75, ŷ = σ(0.75) = 0.679, closer to 1.

written.q: Explain why a single neuron can learn AND but not XOR, and how a hidden layer fixes this.
written.a: AND has one class 1 point (1,1) and three class 0 points, separable by one straight line, so it is linearly separable (e.g. w0 = −6, w1 = w2 = 4 gives 0.0025, 0.119, 0.119, 0.881). XOR's class 1 points (0,1), (1,0) and class 0 points (0,0), (1,1) lie on opposite diagonals, so no single line separates them. A hidden layer with an OR neuron and an AND neuron, combined by an output neuron (OR on, AND off) gives 0, 1, 1, 0: each hidden neuron makes one boundary and the output combines them.

written.q: A 2-3-1 MLP uses ReLU in the hidden layer. Hidden weights (for x<sub>1</sub>, x<sub>2</sub>): (0.5, −1), (1, 1), (−0.5, 0.5); output weights (1, 0.5, 2), output bias −1, sigmoid output. Find the output for x = (1, 2) and the number of weights and biases.
written.a: Hidden z: −1.5, 3, 0.5, so ReLU outputs 0, 3, 0.5. Output z = 0 × 1 + 3 × 0.5 + 0.5 × 2 − 1 = 1.5, ŷ = σ(1.5) = 0.818. Weights 2×3 + 3×1 = 9; biases 3 + 1 = 4.
